opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that you need to understand a lot more of it than most people expect, and the reason is that the bottlenecks move. If you only understand the math of your model, you'll design something that looks beautiful on paper and then runs at 15% utilization on real hardware, and you won't even know why. So my rule of thumb has always been: go one or two layers deeper than the layer you're actually working at.

If I'm designing a training algorithm, I want to understand how it maps onto the accelerator. Where the memory bandwidth goes, what's communication-bound versus compute-bound, how the data loader behaves, what happens when you shard across thousands of devices. I don't necessarily need to write every CUDA kernel myself, but I need enough intuition to know when an idea is going to be expensive in practice versus just expensive in FLOPs on a whiteboard. Those are very different things.

And then there's a practical side. A lot of research progress, especially at the frontier, comes down to how many experiments you can run and how quickly you can trust the results. If your infrastructure is slow or flaky, your research is slow and flaky. So understanding the systems isn't a distraction from research; it's a multiplier on it. Some of the biggest jumps I've seen came from people who could look at a problem and say, "Actually, if we restructure this to fit the hardware better, we get a 5x speedup, and now this whole class of ideas becomes feasible."

That said, you can't go infinitely deep. You don't need to understand transistor physics to do good ML research. The way I decide is basically by asking: where is the thing that's limiting me right now? If it's the algorithm, I stay up there. If it's throughput, memory, or reliability, I go down into the stack until I understand the constraint well enough to work around it or fix it. And over time you build up a mental model of the whole system, so you get faster at spotting which layer the problem actually lives in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding how algorithms map to accelerators and says researchers need not write every CUDA kernel. It does not assert that AI researchers should be able to implement an LLM.

r002.rationale: It recommends going one or two layers deeper and following the current bottleneck, but does not recommend tracing the dependencies of the AI problem to decide how far down the stack to learn.

r003.rationale: It says systems understanding is a multiplier on research and explains that better infrastructure and hardware fit can enable faster experiments and make new ideas feasible.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that you should understand it a lot deeper than feels necessary, and the reason is that the thing that makes the difference between a good researcher and a great one is almost never the idea. Ideas are cheap. Everyone in this field has a notebook full of them. What's expensive is knowing which ideas are actually going to work once they meet the hardware, and you cannot reason about that if the stack below your Python code is a black box to you.

My own path was a bit unusual. When I was a teenager I was interested in poker AI, and there was no infrastructure for that. There was no library you could pip install. So I ended up writing a lot of the systems myself, and the thing I learned was that a huge fraction of what people called "research progress" was actually just "I made the thing run three times faster so I could run three times more experiments." That's not a side effect. That is the research. The person who can iterate faster wins, almost regardless of how clever they are.

So the way I think about it now is in layers. You don't need to be able to write a CUDA kernel from scratch on day one. But you need to know what a kernel is, you need to know roughly what the memory hierarchy looks like, you need to know why your model is memory-bound versus compute-bound, you need to understand what happens when you split a model across eight GPUs and then across eight nodes, and what the interconnect does to you. Because when you propose a new architecture, the first question a serious person will ask is "what does this cost?" and if you can't answer that, your idea is not really an idea yet. It's a wish.

And at Magic, the way we do it is we basically refuse to have the separation. We don't have a research team that throws things over the wall to an engineering team. The people designing the models are the same people who understand why the attention implementation is slow at long context, because that constraint shapes what you're even allowed to think about. Our whole bet is on very long context, and that is not primarily a modeling problem, it's a systems problem that happens to look like a modeling problem from the outside.

The rule I'd give someone starting out is: go one layer deeper than you're comfortable with, and then stay there until you're comfortable, and then go one more. Nobody ever regretted understanding the stack too well. Lots of people have wasted months on an approach that was dead on arrival because they didn't.

r001.rationale: The response recommends understanding kernels and other systems concepts, but does not assert that AI researchers should be able to implement an LLM.

r002.rationale: It advises going one layer deeper and discusses system constraints, but does not recommend choosing depth by tracing the dependencies of the AI problem being solved.

r003.rationale: It says understanding hardware and systems helps researchers identify which ideas will work, iterate faster, and shape viable model designs.

astra-6.text:
I think you work backward from what you’re trying to do. You don’t need to understand every layer of the computing stack equally well, but you want enough understanding of the layers below yours to recognize when they’re constraining you.

If you’re testing a research idea, you might start with a high-level framework and focus on getting the experiment right. If it’s running much slower than you expected, then you need to go deeper: Is the bottleneck loading data, communication between GPUs, or the actual computation? That determines what you should learn next.

The useful skill is being willing to cross those boundaries. You can’t learn everything in advance, but you also don’t want to treat something as a black box forever just because it falls outside your job title.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that AI researchers should be able to implement an LLM.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting from what you are trying to do and investigating bottlenecks, but does not clearly recommend tracing the problem’s dependencies to determine how far down the stack to learn.

r003.rationale: It says lower-layer knowledge helps identify constraints, but does not state that understanding those layers improves research at the top of the stack.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you want to understand at least one layer below the layer you’re working on. If you’re designing learning algorithms, you should understand how those algorithms actually execute: where the compute goes, where the memory goes, and what happens when you distribute them across machines.

You don’t necessarily need to understand every detail of the hardware. But if you treat everything beneath your model as a black box, you can miss research directions because you assume something is too expensive when it’s really just implemented poorly.

So I’d let the problem guide the depth. When you hit a bottleneck, go down another layer until you can explain it. The useful standard isn’t whether you know the whole stack; it’s whether you know enough to tell what’s a fundamental limitation and what you can change.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding algorithm execution and lower stack layers, but never says researchers should be able to implement an LLM.

r002.rationale: It says to let the problem guide depth and to descend another layer when a bottleneck arises until it can be explained, conveying a problem-driven approach to tracing what needs to be understood.

r003.rationale: It says treating lower layers as black boxes can cause researchers to miss directions and that deeper understanding helps distinguish fundamental limits from changeable implementation choices.
